videoIdeas.title: Tariq bin Ziyad burned the ships
videoIdeas.hook: In 711, a man burned his own escape route in front of his entire army. Then he won.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your best-performing original content is Islamic history (the Andalusia post hit 437 views, your top). Nobody else in your competitor set is doing leadership lessons through history — it's your lane and the data proves it lands. Lead with the story, pull the leadership principle out of it.
videoIdeas.script: In 711, a man burned his own escape route in front of his entire army. Then he won. Tariq bin Ziyad crossed into Spain with a few thousand men against an army many times his size. His soldiers looked back at the ships that brought them — the only way home. So he burned them. Not because he was reckless. Because he understood something about people most leaders never will: men fight differently when retreat isn't an option. He didn't give a motivational speech about believing in yourself. He removed the option of failure. That's leadership. Not hyping people up — restructuring the situation so the only way out is forward. Ask yourself where your own 'ships' are. The backup plan you keep looking at. The exit you've mentally reserved. Sometimes the reason you're not moving forward is that going back still feels possible.

visuals.setting: Dark, moody indoor setup or against a plain wall, dim warm lighting. Plain dark top. Low, deliberate energy — you're telling a story, not performing it. Tight framing, chest up.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '711 AD' slams onto the screen over a close, serious face as you say the first line — no smile, slow delivery.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on just the words 'He burned the ships' with a hard cut to your face
Start mid-sentence with '...so he burned them' then rewind to explain
Overlay an old map of the Strait of Gibraltar for the first 3 seconds

videoIdeas.title: Stop memorizing your speech
videoIdeas.hook: If you memorize your speech word for word, you've already lost.
videoIdeas.rationale: You have zero pure public-speaking content in your top posts despite it being a core pillar. Daanish's listicle/teaching format (5 careers, journaling) is pulling huge numbers — practical, teachable, saveable content wins right now. Fill your own gap with a concrete skill.
videoIdeas.script: If you memorize your speech word for word, you've already lost. Here's why. The moment you forget one line, your brain stops listening to the room and starts searching for the next word. You're no longer present — you're retrieving. The audience feels it instantly. You go from a person talking to a person reciting. Instead, memorize three things: your opening line, your closing line, and the three points in between. That's it. The opening so you start strong instead of mumbling. The closing so you land instead of trailing off. And the three points as anchors you speak around, not from. Everything in between should sound like you're figuring it out with them in real time — because that's what makes people lean in. Fluency isn't knowing every word. It's knowing where you're going.

visuals.setting: Clean, brighter setup — standing, slightly wider frame so hand gestures show. Smart-casual. Confident, slightly faster energy than the history piece. Could be filmed as if backstage or near a lectern/mic.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'STOP memorizing your speech' with a hard red cross animation over the word 'memorizing' in the first second.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open of you 'freezing' mid-speech, blank stare, then cut to 'this is why'
Count up 1-2-3 on screen as you name the three things to memorize
Pattern interrupt: start whispering the first line so people turn the volume up

videoIdeas.title: The networking question that actually works
videoIdeas.hook: Stop asking people 'so what do you do.' It's the fastest way to be forgotten.
videoIdeas.rationale: Birdtart's networking-questions video did 975K views — by far the biggest number in your entire competitor set. That's a proven, high-demand topic in this niche with a direct leadership/career angle. There's a clear gap: you're not teaching any practical social or professional skills yet.
videoIdeas.script: Stop asking people 'so what do you do.' It's the fastest way to be forgotten. Everyone asks it, nobody remembers the answer, and you've just reduced a human being to their job title. Here's what to ask instead. 'What are you working on that you're actually excited about right now.' Watch what happens. People light up, because you've given them permission to talk about the thing they care about instead of the thing on their business card. Then shut up and listen. Don't wait for your turn to talk about yourself — most people are so busy preparing their own line that they never actually hear the other person. The ones who get remembered in a room aren't the ones who talked the most. They're the ones who made someone else feel interesting. Be that person.

visuals.setting: Filmed in a 'social' environment if possible — a cafe, event space, or busy-looking backdrop. Smart casual, relaxed, approachable energy. Mid frame. Slightly conversational, like you're giving advice across a table.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'so... what do you do?' with a loud buzzer/wrong-answer X over it as you say the line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-handshake, awkward silence, then cut to camera
On-screen caption that reveals the better question as a 'punchline' at the end
Split-text format: 'DON'T say this / SAY this' as two cards

videoIdeas.title: You can pray and still need help
videoIdeas.hook: Praying about your problem and doing nothing about it are not the same thing.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's short, punchy two-line format ('You can pray and still need help. Both can be true.') hit 20K+ views — short, declarative mindset truths perform well right now. This also matches your bluntest, most quotable captions. Low production, high shareability.
videoIdeas.script: Praying about your problem and doing nothing about it are not the same thing. Somewhere along the way people turned tawakkul into an excuse. 'I'm leaving it to Allah' — while refusing to see the doctor, refusing to study, refusing to have the hard conversation. That's not trust. That's avoidance wearing a prayer cap. The man tied his camel first, then trusted Allah. First. He didn't choose one. He did both. Making dua and making moves are not opposites — they're supposed to happen in the same breath. So pray like it depends on Allah. Then work like it depends on you. Anyone telling you to pick one has misunderstood the deen.

visuals.setting: Simple, honest setup — plain wall, natural light, still frame. Minimal. Calm but firm delivery, not soft. Let the words carry it.
visuals.visualHook: Bold on-screen text of the full first line typed out word by word in silence before you start speaking.
otherHookIdeas: Two-card format matching Dinoo's style: 'You can pray' / 'and still take action'
Hold a long pause on your face before the first word as a pattern interrupt
End on a single text card with the last line for the screenshot/share

videoIdeas.title: Silence isn't neutral
videoIdeas.hook: When you say nothing about an injustice, you haven't stayed neutral. You've picked a side.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Majid Freeman post pulled 289 likes — your highest like count by far — proving your audience responds hard to conviction and speaking out. Saffana and Dinoo both get massive engagement calling things out. This leans into what already works for you, framed as a mindset/character piece rather than a one-off news post.
videoIdeas.script: When you say nothing about an injustice, you haven't stayed neutral. You've picked a side — the side of whoever benefits from your silence. The Prophet ﷺ gave us a ladder: change it with your hand, and if you can't, your tongue, and if you can't, at least hate it in your heart. Notice there's no rung that says 'mind your business.' No level where saying nothing is acceptable. We've convinced ourselves that staying quiet is the safe, mature option. It's not maturity. It's comfort. You're protecting your own peace by pretending the problem isn't yours. But the people who move this world forward were never the quiet, agreeable ones. They were the ones who opened their mouths when it cost them something. Use your tongue. That's the minimum, not the maximum.

visuals.setting: Serious, direct-to-camera, plain dark background. Tight frame. Still. No music or very low. This is a conviction piece — energy is controlled intensity, not shouting.
visuals.visualHook: Open on total silence for 2 seconds with on-screen text 'Silence is a choice.' then you speak.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open with direct eye contact and the full hook line, no intro
On-screen text of the three rungs appearing as you name hand / tongue / heart
Cut the background audio completely for the first line to make 'silence' literal

videoIdeas.title: How to command a room when you walk in
videoIdeas.hook: The people who command a room aren't the loudest. They're the slowest.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is an under-served pillar for you, and 'presence' content is a gap no competitor here is filling directly. Daanish's teaching format proves practical, specific how-to content performs — this is the leadership-presence version of that, highly saveable.
videoIdeas.script: The people who command a room aren't the loudest. They're the slowest. Watch anyone with real presence. They don't rush to fill silence. They don't speak the second a question lands. They pause — and that pause makes everyone wait on them. Speed signals nervousness. Slowness signals control. Three things, quickly. One: slow your walk. People who hurry look like they're answering to someone. Two: slow your speech. The urge to talk fast comes from the fear you'll be interrupted — act like you won't be. Three: hold eye contact one second longer than feels comfortable. That second is where authority lives. You don't command a room by being the biggest voice in it. You command it by being the calmest.

visuals.setting: Walk-and-talk if possible — film yourself entering a space, or standing confidently in an open room. Smart attire. Deliberately slow, grounded movements that demonstrate the point as you make it.
visuals.visualHook: Slow-motion shot of you walking into frame with on-screen text 'watch the walk' before any words.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a long, deliberate pause making the viewer wait — demonstrate it
Number each tip on screen 1/2/3 as fast-save value content
Split-screen: 'rushed' vs 'slow' version of the same entrance

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your top post for views (437) and it's no accident — Islamic history storytelling is clearly your strongest lane and completely differentiates you from the competitor set. The caption opens with a vivid, specific, almost unbelievable hook ('Christians were begging Muslims to come liberate them') that forces a double-take.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments despite 437 views means you never asked anything of the viewer. End the caption with a pointed question or a leadership lesson that invites debate ('Would your people welcome you the way Andalusia welcomed Tariq?'). Also, the caption is cut off mid-sentence ('wasn't built t') — tighten it so the payoff isn't lost.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your second-highest views (369) and your best comment count (5) and likes (45) — proof that personal, relatable, human moments pull your audience in harder per-view than your polished content. The casual, funny caption ('Never running through a park at night ever again 😭') feels real and sparks replies.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This performs on relatability but does nothing for your niche — none of your three pillars show up. Use these personal moments as a Trojan horse: tie the fear/adrenaline back to a mindset point so the engagement actually builds your positioning instead of being a one-off.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Good instinct opening with a universal pain point ('Burnout affects so many of us') and the emoji use breaks up the text well. Naming that it applies beyond medical students was smart — it widens the audience.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 209 views with only 21 likes — this reads as a promo for the Sabr app, and audiences scroll past content that smells like an ad. Lead with your own genuine take on burnout for the first half, earn the attention, and only then mention the app. Right now the value and the pitch are tangled together.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — by far your highest engagement, which tells you plainly: your audience responds to conviction and speaking out on injustice. Opening with the hadith grounds it in authority and the direct call ('Silence is not an option') matches your blunt voice perfectly.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This was a Sidecar (carousel), not a video — and your entire competitor set's top posts are videos. Only 1 comment despite 289 likes suggests people agreed and moved on without a clear action. Convert this energy into a talking-head video and end with a specific ask (share, tag, a concrete step) so the conviction turns into reach, not just likes.
